scenes.title: Maya's morning
scenes.description: Maya, an administrator at a community centre, wakes to her seven o'clock alarm and prepares for the evening photography club. The alarm is an example of ordinary automation.
lines: Meet Maya.
She works as an administrator at a community centre.
This evening, the centre is hosting a photography club and she has a few things to prepare.
At seven, her alarm rings.
Maya chose that time herself.
The phone simply follows her instruction.
A basic alarm doesn't need AI.
As Maya gets ready, she uses other tools that may use AI.
Let's follow her day.

scenes.title: Finding the right photo
scenes.description: Maya searches her own phone gallery for a dog photo for the club poster. Dog photos appear among unrelated pictures. She opens one to check it is the right photo.
lines: Before leaving home, Maya needs a dog photo for the club poster.
She has hundreds of pictures on her phone and can't remember what she called the file.
She types "dog" into photo search.
Pictures of dogs appear, even though she never named those files "dog".
Some photo apps use AI to recognise patterns in pictures and suggest likely matches.
This is called image recognition.
Maya opens a result to make sure it's the photo she wanted.

scenes.title: Getting to the centre
scenes.description: Maya opens a map. Traffic builds on her usual route, changing its estimate to thirty minutes. Another route shows twenty minutes. She checks the route before leaving.
lines: Later, Maya opens a map to plan her journey.
Traffic is building on her usual road.
The map estimates thirty minutes that way or twenty minutes by another route.
Some navigation services use AI to combine current traffic with patterns from earlier journeys.
They use that information to estimate what might happen next.
That's a prediction, not a promise.
Maya checks the route before setting off.

scenes.title: A useful suggestion?
scenes.description: At the community centre, Maya browses camera bags online. A shop suggests another bag. She checks its price and dimensions and sees that the camera will not fit.
lines: At the centre, Maya looks online for a bag to carry the club camera.
After she views a few options, the shop suggests another one.
Some shops use AI to find patterns in what people view and suggest products they might like.
That's a recommendation.
It may be useful, but Maya still has to decide.
She checks the price and size.
The camera is 28 centimetres long, but the bag has only 25 centimetres of space inside.
It won't fit, so she keeps looking.

scenes.title: A missing message
scenes.description: Before the club starts, Maya looks for a booking confirmation email. She finds it in Spam, compares it with her booking record and uses a known contact if she is unsure.
lines: Before the club starts, Maya can't find the booking confirmation email.
She checks Spam, and there it is.
Some email services use AI to look for patterns and other signals when sorting messages.
Putting a message into a group, such as Inbox or Spam, is called classification.
The sorting can be wrong.
Maya compares the email with her booking record.
If something still seems off, she checks through a contact she already knows.
A message isn't safe just because it reached her Inbox.

scenes.title: Ready for the club
scenes.description: Maya stands in the prepared photography room. The photo, map, bag and message return as a visual recap, each paired with Maya's check. Learners are invited to reflect on a familiar tool.
lines: Now the photography room is ready.
Maya found a photo, planned her journey, checked her bag suggestion and found a missing message.
Across her day, some tools may have used AI to recognise, predict, recommend and classify.
But Maya made the decisions.
She checked each result against what she actually needed.
Now think of a tool in your day.
It could be a music app suggesting a song or a streaming service suggesting a film.
What information does it receive?
What does it give you?
What would you check?
Use those questions in the short activity after the film.
